title: The Late Promise
premise: Bram Okonkwo built a celebrated wedding-planning career on the ruins of his own abandoned engagement, orchestrating other people's happily-ever-afters while refusing his own. When his estranged family summons him to a reunion on Harrow Island, he hires Marisol Vega—a ferry-schedule-obsessed marine archivist—to pose as his partner for one weekend. The fake date curdles into something real by dessert, but the reunion's true purpose surfaces: his late grandmother's will ties the family inn, and Bram's inheritance of it, to whoever can prove they'll stay. As the last ferry of the season approaches, Bram must choose between the London career that saved him and Marisol and the island life that might finally let him be seen—ending with him missing the ferry on purpose, signing the deed, and planning one more wedding: their own.
about_author: Astrid Underhill is a former event coordinator who spent a decade watching love arrive on schedule before turning to fiction to write about the kind that doesn't. She lives on a tidal island reachable only at low tide, which she insists is a personality trait.

chapters.title: The Man Who Plans Endings
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. At a flawless society wedding in London, Bram executes a perfect ceremony while privately flinching at every vow—he hasn't attended a wedding as a guest since his own collapsed eight years ago. A call from his sister Nneka summons him to the family reunion on Harrow Island. Beat: polished exterior, hollow center.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram drafts a contract for a fake partner: charming, low-maintenance, gone by Monday. His assistant suggests the woman who keeps correcting the ferry timetables in the café downstairs. Beat: control as armor.

chapters.title: The Ferry Timetable Girl
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol Vega, an archivist cataloguing Harrow Island's maritime records, agrees to the absurd job because it funds her digitization project—and because she recognizes a man rehearsing intimacy like a client pitch. Beat: wary curiosity, mutual recognition of loneliness.

chapters.title: Crossing
chapters.summary: Dual POV. On the ferry, they build their backstory over salt air and bad coffee; Marisol improvises details so specific Bram wonders what she's hiding too. First real laugh. Beat: the con begins feeling like company.

chapters.title: The Inn at Harrow Point
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The Okonkwo family inn is shabby, loud, and full of ghosts—Grandmother Adaeze's portrait presiding over a dining room Bram fled at twenty-two. His mother's greeting is a wound dressed as warmth. Beat: homecoming as excavation.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Dual POV. During the reunion dinner, under pressure from a probing aunt, Bram and Marisol's fabricated how-we-met story turns tender and true by accident. They hold hands without being told to. Beat: the fake date becomes real by dessert.

chapters.title: Adaeze's Will
chapters.summary: Nneka's POV. The lawyer reads the will: the inn goes to whichever grandchild demonstrates commitment to Harrow Point within the year—or it's sold to a resort developer. Nneka, who stayed and sacrificed, resents Bram's sudden return. Beat: inheritance as ultimatum.

chapters.title: Rain Check
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Rain traps them in the boathouse archive; Marisol shows Bram Adaeze's letters revealing she once left her own great love for the island and regretted it quietly for fifty years. Beat: the past offering a warning neither fully hears.

chapters.title: A Career Saved Everything
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Flashback woven into present: how wedding planning rebuilt Bram after public humiliation and heartbreak, and why his ex-fiancé Theo still haunts every aisle he walks. His London firm calls with the biggest contract of his career—due the same week as the will's deadline. Beat: ambition reasserting its claim.

chapters.title: Low Tide Confessions
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Walking the causeway at low tide, Marisol admits she took the fake-date job to avoid her own truth: she turned down a research post abroad to stay near the island archives and her late father's memory. Two liars, honestly matched. Beat: intimacy through confession.

chapters.title: The Reunion Games
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Bram's POV. Family Olympics on the beach force alliances; Bram and Nneka clash publicly over who deserves the inn, and old wounds about Bram's abandonment go verbal and bloody. Marisol defends him fiercely—too fiercely. Beat: the family sees what the couple won't admit.

chapters.title: Kissed by Accident
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. After the fight, adrenaline and lantern light on the bluff; a kiss that no audience requires. Both pull back, terrified, and agree it was 'for consistency.' Beat: denial at full volume.

chapters.title: Theo Arrives
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Bram's ex-fiancé Theo appears at the inn—he's consulting for the resort developer bidding on Harrow Point. Old shame walks in wearing a good coat. Marisol watches Bram shrink back into the man he was. Beat: the past weaponized.

chapters.title: The Pitch
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Theo offers Bram a partnership: leave the island, take the developer's event contract, rebuild the empire they once dreamed of together. It's everything Bram wanted at twenty-five. He says he'll think about it. Beat: temptation with a familiar face.

chapters.title: What Marisol Saw
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol finds Adaeze's final letter—one addressed to 'the grandchild who stays'—and must decide whether to hand it over or keep it, since it could decide the inheritance and expose her own stake in staying. Guilt compounds. Beat: the helper needing help.

chapters.title: Midnight Kitchen
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Sleepless, they cook together in the inn's kitchen at 2 a.m., flour and honesty everywhere. Almost-confession of love interrupted by Nneka, who coldly tells Marisol she's a prop and always was. Beat: happiness sabotaged by doubt.

chapters.title: The Letter Goes Missing
chapters.summary: Nneka's POV. Adaeze's letter disappears from the archive box; suspicion falls on Marisol, whose employment contract with Bram surfaces—fake date exposed to the whole family. Betrayal layered on betrayal. Beat: collapse of every pretense.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Storm closes the causeway; the family trapped together while the developer's offer expires at dawn and the season's last ferry is scheduled for morning if weather permits. Bram confronts Theo, then himself. Beat: everything converging.

chapters.title: The Last Ferry of the Season
chapters.summary: Climax, dual POV. Sun breaks; the ferry sounds its horn. Bram stands at the dock with two tickets' worth of choices: London and the career that saved him, or the island and Marisol, who boards alone rather than ask him to stay. He lets the ferry leave without him. Beat: the choice made in public, at cost.

chapters.title: What the Grandchild Who Stays Signs
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Bram presents Adaeze's recovered letter—Nneka had taken it, testing him—and withdraws from the inheritance contest entirely, proposing instead that the inn become a family cooperative with Nneka at its head. Reconciliation, imperfect and real. Beat: giving up the prize to claim the family.

chapters.title: Second Chances Are for People With Better Timing
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Weeks later, Marisol returns from delivering her father's archive to the mainland, convinced she imagined it all—until she finds Bram on the dock, hired by Nneka to plan the inn's first wedding in years: theirs, eventually, but starting with a stranger's, on purpose, as a guest this time. Beat: the promise kept late but kept.

chapters.title: Epilogue: Off Schedule
chapters.summary: Dual POV. One year later: the inn restored, a small wedding on the lawn, Bram planning it joyfully and Marisol reading vows off a corrected ferry timetable. Adaeze's portrait watches them choose each other daily, not just once. Beat: love as a practice, not an event.
